records.public_claim_text: The IEA highlights that without faster deployment of high-efficiency electric technologies, stronger clean-power expansion and policies targeting fossil fuel phase-out in buildings, operational emissions are unlikely to fall at the pace required to align with climate targets (see further details on fuel use and electrification trends in Sections 4 and 5).

records.public_claim_text: Buildings’ energy intensity Overall, the energy intensity of buildings has reduced by 8.5 per cent since 2015 – less than half the 19 per cent reduction needed to stay on track to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Buildings’ energy intensity Overall, the energy intensity of buildings has reduced by 8.5 per cent since 2015 – less than half the 19 per cent reduction needed to stay on track to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

records.public_claim_text: In 2024, the energy intensity of buildings remained stable, indicating a stagnation in efficiency gains, though factors such as weather are estimated to have had a small effect (IEA 2025e).

records.public_claim_text: The energy intensity of heating has more than halved in the country in the past years as coal has been replaced with electrical systems (EMBER 2025).

records.public_claim_text: However, economic development has led to an increased use of household appliances and air conditioners, driving growing energy consumption in residential buildings (Tsinghua University 2025).

records.public_claim_text: Cooling represents 4 per cent of total energy use in buildings in advanced and emerging economies and since 2015 has grown by 70 per cent (UNEP 2025a).
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Cooling represents 4 per cent of total energy use in buildings in advanced and emerging economies and since 2015 has grown by 70 per cent (UNEP 2025a).

records.public_claim_text: This increase was driven by rising global temperatures, population growth in tropical regions, increasing household incomes, and the intensification of heat island effects through urbanisation (IEA 2025a).

records.public_claim_text: Growing building floor area vs energy demand Overall, between 2015 and 2024, the building energy demand did not grow as fast as the floor area of the global building stock.
records.public_claim_verbatim_quote: Growing building floor area vs energy demand Overall, between 2015 and 2024, the building energy demand did not grow as fast as the floor area of the global building stock.

records.public_claim_text: However, in 2024, progress stalled, with building energy intensity remaining at 129 kWh/m², the expansion of new floor area, population growth and rising demand for energy services such as heating, cooling, appliance use and plug load are potentially offsetting improvements in efficiency gains, particularly in emerging economies experiencing rapid urbanisation and increasing living standards (IEA 2025a).
